title: Tame fixed rings of reduced complete equidimensional local rings and their generic components
statement: Let $(C,\mathfrak m)$ be a nonzero reduced complete Noetherian local ring of characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring]. Suppose that $C$ is equidimensional of finite dimension $e\geq1$, meaning $\dim(C/\mathfrak q)=e$ for every minimal prime $\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Reduced means that no nonzero element is nilpotent. Let a finite group $H$ act by local ring automorphisms on $C$, with $|H|$ invertible in $k=C/\mathfrak m$. Put $B=C^H=\{c\in C:h(c)=c\text{ for all }h\in H\}$, $\mathfrak n=B\cap\mathfrak m$, and $\lambda=k^H$. Then $B$ is a reduced Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$, complete for its $\mathfrak n$-adic topology, and $B/\mathfrak n\to k$ identifies its residue field with $\lambda$. The inclusion $B\hookrightarrow C$ is module-finite [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. The extension $k/\lambda$ is finite separable [def-pc-field-extension] [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension]. Contraction maps minimal primes of $C$ onto the minimal primes of $B$. For every minimal prime $\mathfrak q$ of $C$, with $\mathfrak r=\mathfrak q\cap B$, the induced extension $\operatorname{Frac}(C/\mathfrak q)/\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak r)$ is finite separable and $\dim(B/\mathfrak r)=\dim(C/\mathfrak q)=e$. In particular $B$ is equidimensional of dimension $e$.

source.place: Exposé IV Proposition 2.2.3 (i)(a)–(c), (ii)(a)–(b) and its proof, printed pp.53–54; paragraph 2.2.4 (dimension equality). Completeness of the local invariant ring follows from the Reynolds equality J C ∩ B = J and equivalence of the maximal-ideal topologies for the finite local extension. Component dimensions follow by integral dimension equality; the generic component extensions are the finite étale factors in (ii)(b).

proof.text: Write $d=|H|$. Since $d$ has nonzero image in the residue field of the local ring $C$, it is a unit of $C$. Its inverse $u=d^{-1}$ is fixed by every automorphism, so $u\in B$ and $\sum_{h\in H}h(u)=du=1$. Apply [lem-per-trace-one-noetherian-invariant-finiteness] with $R=C$, $G=H$, and trace-one element $u$. It gives precisely that $B$ is Noetherian and that $C$ is a finitely generated $B$-module. No faithful-action hypothesis is needed.

source.place: Exposé IV Proposition 2.2.3(i)(a), (ii)(a), printed pp.53–54; trace-one generalization already in the DAG.

proof.text: Define $E:C\to B$ by $E(c)=u\sum_{h\in H}h(c)$. Reindexing the sum shows that its values are invariant; it is $B$-linear and $E(b)=b$ for $b\in B$. For every ideal $J\subseteq B$, this gives $E(JC)\subseteq J$ and hence $JC\cap B=J$. A nilpotent element of $B$ is nilpotent in $C$ and therefore zero. If $b\in B\setminus\mathfrak n$, its inverse in $C$ is fixed because $h(b^{-1})=h(b)^{-1}=b^{-1}$; thus it is a unit of $B$. Conversely no element of $\mathfrak n=B\cap\mathfrak m$ is a unit, so $B$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$. Reduction gives an injection $B/\mathfrak n\hookrightarrow k$ with invariant image. For $a\in k^H$, lift $a$ to $c\in C$; then $E(c)$ reduces to $d^{-1}\sum_h h(a)=a$. Thus the image is exactly $\lambda=k^H$.

source.place: Exposé IV Proposition 2.2.3(i)(b),(c) and Reynolds calculation, printed p.53.

proof.text: The ideal $\mathfrak nC$ is finitely generated, since $C$ is Noetherian, and is contained in $\mathfrak m$. Apply [lem-sfb-adic-complete-subideal] with $A=C$, $L=\mathfrak nC$, $K=\mathfrak m$: $C$ is complete for the $\mathfrak nC$-adic topology. Now let $(\bar b_t)_t\in\varprojlim_t B/\mathfrak n^t$. Choose representatives $b_t\in B$. Their images form a compatible system modulo $(\mathfrak nC)^t=\mathfrak n^tC$, so completeness gives $c\in C$ with $c-b_t\in\mathfrak n^tC$ for every $t$. The $B$-linearity of $E$ gives $E(c)-b_t\in\mathfrak n^t$, so $E(c)\in B$ lifts the system. If $b\in\bigcap_t\mathfrak n^t$, then $b\in\bigcap_t(\mathfrak nC)^t=0$. The canonical map $B\to\varprojlim_t B/\mathfrak n^t$ is therefore bijective, which is exactly [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring].

source.place: Tag 090T, lemma-complete-by-sub; Tag 0317, definition-complete; Reynolds retraction of ILO IV 2.2.3.

proof.text: Let $\overline H$ be the image of $H\to\operatorname{Aut}(k)$. This is a finite group acting faithfully on $k$, and $k^{\overline H}=k^H=\lambda$. Apply [lem-wf-finite-field-action-fixed-degree] to $L=k$ and $G=\overline H$. It gives that $k/\lambda$ is finite Galois, in particular finite separable. Passing to the image is necessary because the given action of $H$ on $k$ may have a kernel.

source.place: Tag 09I3, lemma-galois-over-fixed-field; residue field from ILO IV 2.2.3(i)(c).

proof.text: By [lem-dl-a1-finite-invariant-prime-orbits-residues], $B\subseteq C$ is integral and $H$ is transitive on primes with any fixed contraction. Fix a minimal prime $\mathfrak q$ of $C$, and set $\mathfrak r=\mathfrak q\cap B$. Choose a minimal prime $\mathfrak r_0\subseteq\mathfrak r$ using [lem-weil-pbc-prime-contains-minimal-prime]. Lying over [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-lying-over] gives $\mathfrak q_0$ over $\mathfrak r_0$; going up [pqf-lem-going-up] gives $\mathfrak q_1\supseteq\mathfrak q_0$ over $\mathfrak r$. Transitivity makes $\mathfrak q_1$ an $H$-translate of $\mathfrak q$, hence minimal. Thus $\mathfrak q_0=\mathfrak q_1$ and $\mathfrak r_0=\mathfrak r$. Conversely, for any minimal prime $\mathfrak r$ of $B$, lying over gives a prime of $C$ over it. Choose a minimal prime contained in that prime by the same minimal-prime lemma; its contraction is contained in $\mathfrak r$ and hence equals $\mathfrak r$. This proves exactly the asserted surjection on minimal primes.

source.place: Exposé IV Proposition 2.2.3(ii)(a), reduced-case proof, printed p.54; Stacks Tags 0BRI, 00E0, 00GQ, 00GU.

proof.text: Fix $\mathfrak q,\mathfrak r$ as in Step 5. Put $K=\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak r)$ and $S=B\setminus\mathfrak r$. Since $B$ is reduced and $\mathfrak r$ minimal, [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-prime-reduced-localization-field] identifies $B_{\mathfrak r}$ with $K$: its maximal ideal is zero and all nonzero elements of $B/\mathfrak r$ are inverted. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-base-change], $A=K\otimes_B C=S^{-1}C$. This localization is reduced: if $(c/s)^n=0$, some $t\in S$ satisfies $tc^n=0$; then $(tc)^n=0$ in $C$, so $tc=0$ and $c/s=0$. The images of any finite $B$-generating family of $C$ span $A$ over $K$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-dim-algebra-artinian] and then [lem-sfb-reduced-artinian-residue-product] to obtain the canonical finite product of fields $A=\prod_j L_j$. The prime $\mathfrak q$ is disjoint from $S$; [lem-weil-pbc-localization-spectrum-embedding] supplies its corresponding prime $S^{-1}\mathfrak q$ of $A$. In a finite product of fields a prime is a projection kernel (the coordinate idempotents show that exactly one factor survives). Its quotient is thus one field factor $L_i$. The same quotient is $S^{-1}(C/\mathfrak q)$ by the fraction formulas, so, being a field containing $C/\mathfrak q$, it equals $L_i=\operatorname{Frac}(C/\mathfrak q)$.

source.place: Exposé IV Proposition 2.2.3(ii), reduction to a product of fields, printed p.54; Stacks Tags 00EU, 00DK, 00J6, 00JB, 00E3.

proof.text: Apply [lem-per-tame-invariants-arbitrary-base-change] to the $B$-algebra $C$ and scalar algebra $K$. Its hypotheses hold because $H$ acts $B$-linearly and $d^{-1}\in B$. It gives $A^H=K\otimes_B C^H=K$, with the canonical scalar inclusion. In particular $K\hookrightarrow A$; the algebra is nonzero since Step 6 gives its field factor. Every prime of $A$ contracts to $(0)$ in $K$, so [lem-dl-a1-finite-invariant-prime-orbits-residues], applied to $A$ and its full invariant subring $K$, shows that $H$ permutes the field factors transitively. Let $D\subseteq H$ stabilize the factor $L_i$. Projection gives $A^H\simeq L_i^D$: an invariant tuple is determined by its $i$-coordinate, and for $x\in L_i^D$ its inverse tuple has coordinate $h(x)$ at the factor $h(i)$. This is well-defined because $h(i)=h'(i)$ implies $h'^{-1}h\in D$, and it is invariant because $g(h(x))=(gh)(x)$. The identification takes the scalar copy of $K$ to its given image in $L_i$. Pass to the finite image $\overline D\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(L_i)$; it acts faithfully and $L_i^{\overline D}=L_i^D=K$. Now [lem-wf-finite-field-action-fixed-degree] shows that $L_i/K$ is finite separable. These are precisely the component fraction fields asserted in the item.

source.place: Exposé IV Proposition 2.2.3(ii)(b), last paragraph, printed p.54; Stacks Tags 0BRI and 09I3, Reynolds base change as in 0H36.

proof.text: The map $B/\mathfrak r\hookrightarrow C/\mathfrak q$ is injective by the definition of contraction. It is integral: for $c\in C$, the polynomial $\prod_{h\in H}(T-h(c))$ is monic with coefficients in $B$ and vanishes at $c$; reducing modulo $\mathfrak q$ gives a monic relation over $B/\mathfrak r$ for every element of $C/\mathfrak q$. Therefore [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-dimension-equal] gives $\dim(B/\mathfrak r)=\dim(C/\mathfrak q)=e$. By Step 5 every minimal prime of $B$ occurs this way, so all its component dimensions are $e$. Finally every finite chain of prime ideals of $B$ lies over a minimal prime contained in its first member, by [lem-weil-pbc-prime-contains-minimal-prime], and is a chain in that component quotient. Its length is at most $e$. Conversely chains in any component quotient are chains in $B$, giving $\dim B\ge e$. Thus $\dim B=e$ and $B$ is equidimensional, as required.
